item.title: GLM-5.4: Toward generalized coding with our first loop transformer
item.description:
Source: z.ai

Top Comment:

I love the transparency, or at least given technical details, that Zhipu provide - a refreshing change from the locked-down approach of the western companies, and an interesting glimpse into the direction of SOTA LLMs.

Looped Transformers are an obvious direction even if there are still problems to be worked out. The original Transformer is a bit like an unrolled for loop, and rather unnaturally pairs different sets of weights, both for attention and feed forward (knowledge) with different "layers" (aka loop iterations). Far more natural is to strive for something more like our brain's thalamo-cortical loop and association cortex, where "thought" is iterative and there are no restrictions as to what patterns/knowledge get applied when.

A similar idea has been explored before ("Universal Transformer", 2019), seemingly going nowhere, but perhaps "necessity is the mother of invention" and compute-starved Chinese companies are finding a way to make it work.

item.title: Nespresso's project to reduce grams of coffee per capsule
item.description:
Source: alvinbunk.wordpress.com

Top Comment:

Not hard to imagine: that there's some way to manipulate roast levels, grind size, pressure, time, volume extracted etc. to extract a higher TDS (total dissolved solids) from the same amount of coffee in a pod. There are a lot of variables to play with and at Nestlé scale they have the resources to test it (albeit that they already have done so to a huge degree so there's unlikely to be much left to gain here).

Harder to imagine: that it will taste good. We don't want to extract everything from the bean. It's known in specialty espresso that at some point targeting higher TDS will start to result in worse flavor as you will have extracted the tasty stuff already (and all the caffeine) and what's left is bitter/astringent aromatics.

Aside: if anyone wants to get deeper into the science behind coffee I highly recommend this book:

https://www.intechopen.com/books/8952

It's a collection of articles especially focused on growing but also other areas.

item.title: Yes, 17M lines of Lean is a lot
item.description:
Source: micjm.com

Top Comment:

What are peoples' takes on why LLMs struggle to write things in a human-readable way? I've watched Astra and the like write PR descriptions that are middle-school level: as if it struggles to distinguish what it knows (having read the code, having done the debugging) and what someone who hasn't read the code and hasn't participated in the debugging (his target audience) knows. It'll make references to parts of the solution, or of the problem being solved, without contextualizing it, making the references useless, serving only to add confusion to the text.

Terence Tao's take was that LLMs don't understand what is trivial (in a proof, for example) and what is interesting and novel: it gives everything equal weight, or, in Tao's paraphrased words, the LLM will talk at length about something trivial and then write only a single sentence about something novel.

I wonder what peoples' intuition about this is.

item.title: Don't keep your SSH keys on disk
item.description:
Source: jola.dev

Top Comment:

While in theory, this adds at least some small layer of protection, I have doubts that it adds anything meaningful to stop a smart attacker.

The problem here is that everything is running as your user, so it's all the same security sphere.

You may be thinking, "But Bitwarden requires me to approve each key request". Problem is that if the attacker is already running as your user, which I'm assuming here because to steal your bare keys, they'd already need to be. This means they can also hit the approve button for you.

Ok, now you say "But it requires touchID!". Maybe that gets you just a little bit of protection, but...

The next idea is to just steal the decrypted key out of RAM. This requires a little bit of effort, because you generally can't attach to a sibling process without root on Linux with default configs. This will only delay things slightly. Attaching to your child is allowed, so all an attacker needs to do is replace your launch shortcut/service for Bitwarden with a thin wrapper that makes the attacker the parent process, and then they can just ptrace it and steal the decrypted key next startup. On Mac, where the ptrace path isn't viable due to disallowing ptrace of signed binaries by default, you could just replicate the Bitwarden GUI as a wrapper and steal the master password at startup.

If you really want to protect your keys from attacks like this, you need a real hardware device with OOB signaling.

item.title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file
item.description:
Source: huggingface.co

We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.

To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):

- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6

- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4

- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0

- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6

- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9

Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below

(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):

- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7

- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8

- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8

Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork: (https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp)

Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.

Top Comment:

I've been skeptical of these high compute QAT style quant efforts because they tend to over optimize on benchmark-like datasets, so in real usage they don't quite deliver the "almost as good" guarentee the benchmark comparisions suggest.

This project actually does the sort of basic checks I want (and typically don't get)! They show results on multiple types of long horizon tasks (not just coding etc.) and even use the words "held out" a few times :)
